claims.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).
claims.evidence: Assume 2≤m≤n and apply FillColumns to the n×m transpose, writing p=n and q=m. Its proof does not require p≤q: a column rotates at most p−1 times; with f underfull columns, each q buffer-row rotations decreases the wrong-body potential by at least f/2; and in each dyadic range of f the potential is at most f(p−1). Hence each of O(log q) phases costs O(pq), while all column rotations cost O(pq). FloatMinimums adds O(pq) and leaves precisely the state in Claim 6 after transposing back. Claim 6 completes it in O(mN), so this route costs O(N log m+mN)=O(mN). The authorized source independently proves O(N log n). Taking the better route gives O(N·min{m,log n}); symmetry gives the stated bound. One-dimensional sortable boards take O(N). The checker exhaustively corroborated the dimension-reversed FillColumns/FloatMinimums step on all 720 states of a tall 3×2 board.
claims.search_method: Independent potential analysis and reduction to Claim 6, supplemented by exhaustive exact-state simulation of the tall 3×2 phase.

claims.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
claims.evidence: Claim 0 gives O(Ns)=O(N) for each fixed s. With dimensions s×t, translating the sorted board by floor(t/2) columns and floor(s/2) rows is sortable and, by Claim 2, has exact distance s·floor(t/2)+t·floor(s/2)=Ω(st)=Ω(N). Thus the upper and lower bounds match as t tends to infinity.
claims.witness: For every fixed s≥2, the family obtained by the simultaneous half-column and half-row translation has distance s·floor(t/2)+t·floor(s/2).
claims.search_method: Direct asymptotic comparison using the independently proved upper bound and exact translation-distance formula.

claims.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
claims.evidence: Cyclic distance is 1-Lipschitz under a unit step. A row push therefore changes H by at most n and no column push changes H; sorting requires at least ceil(H/n) row pushes. Symmetrically it requires at least ceil(V/m) column pushes, and the two counts add. For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), giving the claimed lower bound. Rotating each of the m rows d_n(a) times and each of the n columns d_m(b) times in shortest reverse directions attains it. If pn is extended by +∞ for an unsortable configuration, the inequality there is immediate. Exact BFS checked the certificate on all 720 configurations of the 2×3 board and checked the formula for all six global translations.
claims.witness: The matching upper-bound sequence rotates every row through the shortest inverse of a and every column through the shortest inverse of b.
claims.search_method: Per-push Lipschitz proof plus exhaustive exact verification on the complete 2×3 state graph.

claims.claim: For m,n≥2, a sharper general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
claims.evidence: The source's parity characterization gives exactly Q reachable configurations. There are d nominal directed push labels. A shortest word contains no adjacent generator followed by its inverse, so the number of configurations at distance at most L is no greater than 1+d·sum_{i=0}^{L−1}(d−1)^i=1+d((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2). Duplicate direction labels on a length-two line only enlarge this word count; for m,n≥2 no nominal push is the identity. Setting L=D, comparing the ball size with Q, and rearranging gives exactly the displayed ceiling. Integer-power checks confirmed the bound against complete BFS diameters for 2×2, 2×3, 3×2, and 3×3, including the odd×odd reachable count 9!/2.
claims.search_method: Exact Cayley-ball counting argument, with integer-only finite checks on four complete state graphs.

claims.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
claims.evidence: Exact BFS with the seven distinct position permutations generated by unit pushes reached all 720 configurations. Its level histogram was (1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3), proving diameter 7. The stated reversed-row configuration is at distance 7 and is produced by the supplied seven-push word. Exhausting all six global translations gave distances 0,2,2,3,5,5, agreeing with Claim 2 and establishing maximum 5.
claims.witness: The distance-7 configuration has rows (3,2,1) and (6,5,4). From the identity it is produced by R1-left, C1, R1-left, C1, C3, R1-right, C1.
claims.search_method: Complete exact-arithmetic breadth-first search of the 2×3 Cayley graph, followed by exhaustive evaluation of all global translations.

claims.claim: On an a×b board with a,b≥2, every even permutation of the positions of one specified row can be performed in O(ab) unit pushes while fixing every other position; the analogous statement holds for a specified column. If a or b is even, every permutation of a specified row or column can be performed this way.
claims.evidence: Factor an even row permutation π as συ where σ and υ are involutions having the same number k of transpositions. Two SwapPairs calls with opposite side-effect directions apply σ and υ and cancel the body shifts of the same k auxiliary columns. They fix every off-row position and cost O(ka+b)=O(ab). If b is even, one b-cycle row push changes the parity and reduces an arbitrary odd permutation to the even case. If b is odd and a is even, factor an odd permutation as συτ. The first two calls cancel; the τ call leaves one cyclic shift on the a−1 off-row cells of an auxiliary column. Since a−1 is odd, that cycle is even and its inverse is supplied by the already-proved even-column construction. Transposition gives columns, and cyclic conjugation gives any specified line. A literal SwapPairs simulator verified every applicable row permutation, and the transposed even-column cases, for boards 2×2, 2×3, 3×2, 3×3, 4×3, and 3×4.
claims.witness: The construction is the pair of opposite-direction SwapPairs calls for even permutations, with one parity-changing row push or one corrected auxiliary-body cycle in the odd cases.
claims.search_method: Independent positional-permutation proof and exhaustive constructive simulation over all relevant line permutations in six small dimensions.

claims.claim: Let 2≤m≤n and N=mn. If every token whose target column is not 1 lies in its target row and the m target-column-1 tokens occupy column 1, then every sortable such board can be sorted in O(mN) pushes.
claims.evidence: When a dimension is even, Claim 5 exactly corrects the buffer column in O(N) and then each of m rows in O(N). Suppose both dimensions are odd. Sortability makes the whole position permutation even. If the required buffer-column permutation β is even, apply it; the ensuing row corrections have even total parity. Apply each even row correction directly and factor every odd one into an even correction followed by the same adjacent horizontal transposition. Two such transpositions on adjacent rows equal a product of two four-push L-shaped commutators; for nonadjacent rows, multiplying these adjacent-row gadgets along a path cancels all intermediate transpositions. Pairing all residuals costs O(m²)≤O(N). If β is odd, the row-correction product is odd. Choose an odd row correction, factor β into an even column permutation followed by an adjacent vertical transposition P through that row, and factor an adjacent horizontal transposition T from its row correction. P followed by T is one L-shaped 3-cycle and hence one four-push commutator. The remaining correction on that row is even, and all other odd corrections pair as before. Total cost is O(mN). Exact checks found the two-commutator identity, verified every nonadjacent telescoping identity on a 9×5 grid, and exhausted all qualifying 2×3 and 3×3 configurations.
claims.witness: For adjacent rows, the checker exhibits the product of the commutator at the upper-left corner using left/up directions and the inverse commutator at the lower-right corner using right/down directions; its net effect is exactly the two horizontal transpositions.
claims.search_method: Complete parity-case proof, exact symbolic commutator algebra, and exhaustive checks of all qualifying small-board states.

target_evidence: The exact target requests asymptotically tight bounds for the general Torus Puzzle push number, thereby closing the full multiplicative Θ(log max{m,n}) gap. The verified draft proves the improved upper bound O(N·min{s,log t}) and a matching Θ(N) classification for every fixed s. This is material progress, but it is incomplete: when s grows, and in particular for balanced boards where s≥log t, the verified counting lower bound remains Θ(N) in scale while the upper bound can remain Θ(N log t). Thus the requested general tight classification is not established. The final writeup explicitly calls the result partial and does not claim otherwise, so claimed_resolution=PARTIAL is accurate.
